title: Join traps and cross joins
summary: Why totals double, how to stop it, and when every-row-with-every-row is what you want.

steps.title: The row-explosion trap
body: Appointment 1 has **two** prescriptions and **one** invoice of 120. Join all three:
JOIN prescriptions AS pr ON pr.appointment_id = a.id
JOIN invoices AS i ON i.appointment_id = a.id
Joining a row to *many* rows copies it. Now `SUM(i.amount)` says 240, and the finance team says you're wrong.
- **Aggregate before joining**: total each child table in a subquery, then join the totals (one row each).
- **COUNT(DISTINCT ...)** for counts (it can't fix sums: two different 120s would merge).

code: JOIN prescriptions AS pr ON pr.appointment_id = i.appointment_id;

steps.title: Fix the doctor report
prompt: This report should show each doctor's **name**, number of **appointments**, and number of **prescriptions**, but the appointment counts are inflated by the join to prescriptions.
Fix it. Only doctors with at least one appointment are needed.
- `doctors(id, name, specialty, ward_id, mentor_id)`: `ward_id` is NULL for a doctor without a ward; `mentor_id` points at another doctor
- `patients(id, name, born, ward_id)`: `ward_id` is NULL for outpatients
- `appointments(id, patient_id, doctor_id, day, status)`: status is `done`, `cancelled` or `booked`
starter: SELECT d.name, COUNT(a.id) AS appointments, COUNT(pr.id) AS prescriptions
JOIN appointments AS a ON a.doctor_id = d.id
LEFT JOIN prescriptions AS pr ON pr.appointment_id = a.id
solution: SELECT d.name, COUNT(DISTINCT a.id) AS appointments, COUNT(pr.id) AS prescriptions
JOIN appointments AS a ON a.doctor_id = d.id
LEFT JOIN prescriptions AS pr ON pr.appointment_id = a.id

steps.title: Aggregate first, then join
body: For sums, pre-aggregate each child table so it has **one row per key**, then join:
SELECT a.doctor_id, SUM(i.amount) AS billed, SUM(rx.n) AS prescriptions
JOIN invoices AS i ON i.appointment_id = a.id
LEFT JOIN (SELECT appointment_id, COUNT(*) AS n
The subquery in `FROM` (a **derived table**) collapses prescriptions to one row per appointment, so nothing gets copied. You'll write a lot more of these in the next module.

steps.title: Billing that adds up
prompt: Return each **specialty** with its correct invoiced **revenue** and its number of **prescriptions**. Make sure revenue is not inflated by appointments that have several prescriptions.
- `doctors(id, name, specialty, ward_id, mentor_id)`: `ward_id` is NULL for a doctor without a ward; `mentor_id` points at another doctor
- `patients(id, name, born, ward_id)`: `ward_id` is NULL for outpatients
- `appointments(id, patient_id, doctor_id, day, status)`: status is `done`, `cancelled` or `booked`
solution: SELECT d.specialty, SUM(i.amount) AS revenue, COALESCE(SUM(rx.n), 0) AS prescriptions
JOIN appointments AS a ON a.id = i.appointment_id
JOIN doctors AS d ON d.id = a.doctor_id
LEFT JOIN (SELECT appointment_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM prescriptions GROUP BY appointment_id) AS rx

steps.title: CROSS JOIN: every combination
body: `CROSS JOIN` pairs **every** row of one table with **every** row of the other. 3 days × 8 doctors = 24 rows. It has no ON.
That sounds useless, until you need a **grid**: every doctor for every day, including the days they saw nobody.
SELECT d.name, c.day, COUNT(a.id) AS seen
LEFT JOIN appointments AS a ON a.doctor_id = d.id AND a.day = c.day
Without the cross join, a doctor with no appointments on a day has no row for it, and a chart shows a gap instead of a zero.
> **Watch out:** `FROM a, b` with a forgotten WHERE is an *accidental* cross join. On two big tables it's billions of rows.

steps.title: Ward rota grid
prompt: Build the grid for the ward dashboard: **every ward** for **every clinic day**, with the number of appointments that day for patients **in that ward** (**appointments**, 0 when none). Order by ward **name** then **day**.
- `doctors(id, name, specialty, ward_id, mentor_id)`: `ward_id` is NULL for a doctor without a ward; `mentor_id` points at another doctor
- `patients(id, name, born, ward_id)`: `ward_id` is NULL for outpatients
- `appointments(id, patient_id, doctor_id, day, status)`: status is `done`, `cancelled` or `booked`
solution: SELECT w.name, c.day, COUNT(a.id) AS appointments
LEFT JOIN patients AS p ON p.ward_id = w.id
LEFT JOIN appointments AS a ON a.patient_id = p.id AND a.day = c.day
